title: the congregation
hook: the congregation; why Sikhs never practice alone for long

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turban, a crown you tie yourself. Your line was carry yourself like it. Which room did you walk into with your head up? Day thirteen.

You've probably noticed this about yourself. Around certain people you're funnier, kinder, braver. Around others you're more anxious, more cynical, quicker to gossip. Nobody told you to change. The room just did it to you. Parents know this. It's why they want to meet your friends. Coaches know it. Anyone who's tried to quit something while their whole crowd kept doing it knows it. We become, a little at a time, like the people we sit with. Five hundred years ago the Gurus built that simple fact into the center of Sikh life. Today, the word for the company you keep.
screen: `FUNNIER AROUND SOME PEOPLE.` → `ANXIOUS AROUND OTHERS.` → `WE BECOME OUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Sangat. The congregation. The community gathered together. It comes from a root meaning to be together, to keep company. You'll often hear it as sadh sangat, the company of the holy, or satsangat, the true company. Everywhere Guru Nanak traveled, the stories say, he left a sangat behind: a small group of people who met to sing the hymns, share food and look after one another. Long before there were grand buildings, there were these circles of ordinary people. So what makes a sangat true? The scripture asks that very question. In paraphrase, the answer comes back simple: the true congregation is where the one name is spoken. Not where the building is finest or the people are richest. Where people gather around the name. Sikhs speak about the sangat with a startling kind of respect. There's a long tradition that the Guru is present wherever the sangat gathers, and that the voice of the congregation, deciding together, carries real weight. That's why so much of Sikh life happens with others: singing together, eating in one row together, doing seva together, bowing before the scripture together. Not because solitude is bad. Simran on your own breath matters. But the Gurus seem to have known that a person alone will drift, and a person in good company will be carried, the way a small boat is carried by a current. And here's the practical wisdom inside it. You can't always choose your family or your coworkers. But you can choose, at least some of the time, whose company you seek out. The tradition says: choose people who make you remember what's real.
screen: `SANGAT — THE COMPANY YOU KEEP.` · `NANAK LEFT A CIRCLE BEHIND.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `A PERSON ALONE DRIFTS.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY CARRIES YOU.`

segments.voice: Settle, and bring to mind the people you spend the most time with. Not to judge them. Just notice. Who do you leave feeling lighter? Who helps you remember what matters? Picture one of them clearly. Let yourself feel grateful for them, and let that gratitude sit for a while. The bell holds the time.
Sangat. The congregation, the company you keep. The circle gathered around the one name. Thirteenth word.
Your line: good company. Today, reach out to one person who brings out the best in you, and tell them so. Day thirteen.

screen: `DAY 13 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOOR OF THE GURU.`

howItsDone: Sikhs gather as a sangat in the gurdwara to sing kirtan, listen to the scripture, pray Ardas and eat langar together; many also meet in homes for readings and hymn-singing.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the congregation, the company gathered together.

trapdoor: what you thought: the people at church.
what it means: the company you keep, gathered around the one name, which shapes who you become.
what a scholar hears: the scripture defines the true congregation as the place where the one name is spoken, and Sikh tradition holds that the Guru is present in the sangat.
